---
# The Department of Ordinary Sounds

The first sound my mother asked me to bring her was the kitchen drawer.

“Not the cutlery,” she said. “The drawer itself.”

I knew which one she meant. In the house where I grew up, the drawer next to the stove had a wooden runner that swelled in summer. You had to lift the handle as you pulled. If you forgot, the drawer would come halfway out and stop with a sound like someone clearing his throat before disagreeing.

The house had been sold twelve years earlier. My mother was about to turn eighty, and I had asked what she wanted for her birthday. I had been expecting her to say slippers.

“Do you want me to see if the people who live there now will let me record it?”

“Oh, they’ll have fixed it by now,” she said, and went back to peeling her pear.

At the time I worked for the municipal archive, where we had exactly one recording of a drawer. It was in a forty-minute interview with a retired midwife who stopped halfway through to get a photograph. For years, researchers had skipped those eleven seconds to get to the part about the maternity ward. I put on headphones and listened. The drawer was metal. There was a little rolling noise at the end, possibly a pencil.

I brought the recording to my mother anyway.

“No,” she said. “But play it again. I like how she keeps talking from across the room.”

That should have been the end of it. Instead, I spent a Saturday visiting secondhand furniture shops. The dealers were happy to let me open their drawers, though one followed me around afterward, rubbing candle wax on everything I had touched. I came home with seventeen recordings, none of them right, and an oak bedside table I hadn’t meant to buy.

By then I was interested in what else the archive might be missing. We had the high school band playing at the opening of the bypass, the mayor’s speech, and the scissors going through the ribbon. We didn’t have the rattle of the old bus that took people into town before the bypass opened. I asked our director if I could put out a call for ordinary sounds.

“As long as you don’t call it a department,” she said. “Departments have budgets.”

By the end of the first week, the Department of Ordinary Sounds had received six recordings of rain, a dog drinking from a mop bucket, and a ninety-minute cassette labeled *Gill’s boiler, possibly October*. Gill had apparently set up a recorder to catch a noise the plumber insisted she was imagining. At minute eighty-three there was a tremendous knock, followed by a woman shouting, “There! You bastard!”

I wanted to put that one in the listening room. Our director said we’d need Gill’s permission.

A woman named Nadia brought us the sound of her father preparing an orange. She had recorded it by accident while trying to get him to tell a story about his childhood. He refused, on the grounds that she already knew it. On the recording there was the scratch of his thumbnail breaking the skin, then the small wet sounds of the peel coming away. In the background a radio announcer read the shipping forecast.

“Do you know what he did after that?” Nadia said. “He gave me the whole orange. I was thirty-four. I’d come to tell him I was getting divorced, and I never got around to it.”

I asked if she wanted that in the catalog description.

“God, no,” she said. “Put down that it was a big orange.”

Not everyone wanted a sound preserved. A man who had spent forty years repairing shoes came in to hear a recording of his old stitching machine. After a few seconds he took the headphones off.

“Is that the whole thing?”

“There’s another two minutes.”

“I know what it does,” he said. He asked if we had anything from the public pool. He used to swim on Tuesdays, when the shop was closed. We found a recording made for a school project and sat together listening to children yell underneath the huge, hollow noise of the ventilation system. When I offered him the headphones again, he said he preferred it coming out of the little computer speakers. It sounded farther away, which was how he used to hear it from the warm bench where he put on his socks.

I never found the kitchen drawer. What I did find, while looking through my own files, was a video I’d taken in my mother’s flat. I was trying to show her how to send a video. The camera pointed at the table for most of it. We were having tea. At one point she said, “Look, that’s you,” and I said, “No, that’s my thumb.”

She laughed once, very suddenly, and set her cup down.

I knew the cup by the sound. It was the heavy green one with a foot just narrow enough to sit inside the rim of its saucer. When she set it down carelessly, it struck the rim first, then slid into place.

For her birthday I brought the video and a pear cake. She watched the video twice.

“You had a terrible time teaching me that,” she said.

“You kept taking pictures of your knees.”

“They looked all right in those trousers.”

Then she asked me to send her the video, so I did. While I cut the cake, she propped her phone against the sugar bowl and tried to send a video back. She wanted to do it without my looking. I kept my eyes on the cake, even when I heard her mutter that she’d got the ceiling again.

Later, on the bus home, I watched what she’d sent. There were eight seconds of the ceiling, then a view of my hands cutting two uneven slices. From somewhere off camera my mother asked for the smaller one. While I was still deciding which to give her, her hand came into the frame and took the bigger slice. I’d been standing right there and hadn’t noticed. I watched it again.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A carefully shaped literary short story built around a family relationship and an archive of everyday sounds.

## Grounded reading
The narrator’s voice is observant and gently comic, with feeling held in small details rather than explained outright: a drawer that sounds like it is about to disagree, a mother photographing her knees, a hand taking the bigger slice. The story’s pathos comes from the mismatch between what can be recorded and what matters in being together; the narrator fails to find the old drawer but recognizes the familiar sound of the cup. Its invitation is to listen closely to ordinary life without assuming that preservation gives us ownership or full understanding of it.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds domestic sounds, family memory, and the work of an archive, alongside the boundaries people set around what should be recorded or cataloged. Repeatedly, sounds matter because of the relationships around them: the mother’s cup, Nadia’s father peeling an orange, and the shoe repairer’s preferred distance from the pool recording. The ending gives priority to an unplanned, imperfect exchange over the narrator’s original search for a sound.

## Evidence line
> I knew the cup by the sound.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the story’s recurring attention to ordinary sounds and restrained tenderness is distinctive and coherently carried through its resolution.
